title: Hemodialysis Access Protection: Protect the Lifeline
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: An AV fistula or graft is a critical vascular access. Protect it from compression and unnecessary invasive procedures, assess patency, and escalate loss of flow, bleeding, infection, or distal ischemia promptly.
recognize: A change or loss of the expected thrill/bruit, new swelling, redness, drainage, cool painful fingers, or prolonged bleeding can indicate access compromise.
priorities: Assess the access before and after dialysis-related care per role and protect the limb from avoidable compression or trauma.
Escalate absent flow, uncontrolled bleeding, or ischemic symptoms immediately.
assessMonitor: Monitor thrill/bruit when within role, access appearance, distal perfusion, bleeding, and infection cues.
interventions: Use the access only according to dialysis-team/facility policy and protect dressings and puncture sites after treatment.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs can increase post-dialysis bleeding risk; review the medication profile when bleeding persists.
teaching: Patients should protect the access arm and promptly report loss of vibration, bleeding, swelling, or signs of infection.
delegationScope: Dialysis access cannulation and specialized management require competency and policy authorization; PN/LVN scope varies by state and setting.
examTrap: Using the dialysis access as routine venous access because it is easy to see.
oneLinePearl: Protect the access; loss of flow is an emergency cue.

title: Intradialytic Hypotension: Symptoms Matter Before the Number
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Dizziness, nausea, cramping, weakness, chest symptoms, or altered mentation during hemodialysis can signal poor tolerance or hypotension. Stop treating the session as routine and escalate according to dialysis protocol.
recognize: Symptoms may occur with excessive fluid removal, autonomic dysfunction, cardiac disease, or medication effects.
priorities: Assess BP, symptoms, perfusion, and dialysis status and notify the dialysis RN/provider per protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, HR, mental status, symptoms, ultrafiltration status, weight, and response to interventions.
interventions: Follow the dialysis unit's ordered protocol for positioning, ultrafiltration adjustment, and fluid management; do not independently change the prescription.
medicationSafety: Antihypertensive timing may affect dialysis tolerance and should be reviewed with the dialysis team rather than changed independently.
teaching: Patients should report dizziness, nausea, cramping, chest discomfort, or unusual weakness during treatment immediately.
delegationScope: Dialysis prescription changes and ultrafiltration decisions are not routine PN/LVN autonomous decisions.
examTrap: Assuming dizziness is expected and waiting for the session to end.

title: Dialysis Infection: Access and System Changes Need Fast Escalation
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Fever, chills, access redness/drainage, catheter tenderness, or rigors during dialysis can indicate serious infection or bacteremia. Treat new systemic symptoms as urgent, especially with a dialysis catheter.
recognize: Central venous dialysis catheters carry higher bloodstream-infection risk than permanent AV access.
priorities: Assess the patient and access, notify the dialysis RN/provider, and follow culture/sepsis pathways when indicated.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, BP, HR, mental status, access findings, and symptoms during treatment.
interventions: Maintain strict aseptic technique and follow unit protocols for catheter/access care and suspected infection.
medicationSafety: Do not administer antibiotics through a questionable access route without appropriate evaluation and order review.
teaching: Patients should report fever, chills, redness, drainage, or tenderness around dialysis access promptly.
delegationScope: Dialysis catheter access/manipulation is competency- and policy restricted.
examTrap: Treating catheter-site redness as a minor skin issue in a febrile dialysis patient.
oneLinePearl: A dialysis access infection can become bloodstream infection quickly.

title: Dialysis Fluid Overload: Weight, Lungs, and Oxygenation Tell the Story
bottomLine: Rapid weight gain, edema, orthopnea, crackles, hypertension, and increasing oxygen need can indicate fluid overload between dialysis treatments. Acute respiratory distress requires urgent escalation.
recognize: Missed dialysis, excess fluid/sodium intake, cardiac dysfunction, and loss of residual renal function can worsen volume overload.
priorities: Assess respiratory status and hemodynamics first, compare weight with the prescribed dialysis plan, and escalate deterioration.
assessMonitor: Trend weight, edema, lung findings, BP, oxygenation, dyspnea, and urine output when applicable.
interventions: Position for breathing, provide ordered support, reinforce fluid/sodium plan, and coordinate urgent dialysis evaluation when indicated.
medicationSafety: Do not independently increase diuretics or alter dialysis medications when severe fluid overload develops.
teaching: Daily weights and the dialysis team's individualized fluid plan help identify rising volume before crisis.
delegationScope: Weights may be delegated; interpretation of decompensation requires licensed clinical judgment.
examTrap: Waiting for dramatic leg edema while respiratory symptoms worsen.
oneLinePearl: In dialysis patients, breathing and weight trends reveal volume trouble early.

title: Dialysis Patient With Hyperkalemia Cues: Rhythm Risk Is Immediate
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Missed dialysis, weakness, paresthesias, palpitations, bradycardia, or ECG abnormalities can signal dangerous hyperkalemia. Cardiac instability requires emergency escalation rather than routine scheduling advice.
recognize: Dietary potassium, tissue breakdown, acidosis, medications, and missed or inadequate dialysis can contribute.
priorities: Obtain cardiac monitoring/ECG and emergency clinical evaluation according to the patient's condition and orders.
assessMonitor: Monitor rhythm, potassium results when available, neuromuscular symptoms, dialysis history, and medication contributors.
interventions: Prepare for ordered hyperkalemia stabilization and urgent dialysis when indicated.
medicationSafety: Do not use chronic potassium binders as a substitute for emergency stabilization in an unstable patient.
teaching: Patients should understand which symptoms and missed treatments require urgent contact.
delegationScope: Emergency recognition/escalation is within nursing responsibility; definitive dialysis prescription remains specialist-managed.
examTrap: Sending an unstable patient home to attend the next regular dialysis appointment.
oneLinePearl: Hyperkalemia is a rhythm emergency before it is a diet problem.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. emergency hyperkalemia and dialysis safety principles

title: Peritoneal Dialysis Peritonitis: Cloudy Effluent Is a Red Flag
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Cloudy peritoneal dialysis effluent, abdominal pain, fever, nausea, or new systemic illness can indicate peritonitis and requires prompt dialysis-team evaluation.
recognize: Exit-site infection and breaks in exchange technique increase infection risk.
priorities: Do not discard potentially diagnostic effluent if the dialysis protocol calls for sampling; notify the dialysis team promptly.
assessMonitor: Assess effluent clarity, abdominal pain, temperature, exit-site findings, BP/HR, and GI symptoms.
interventions: Maintain aseptic exchange technique and follow the prescribed specimen/treatment pathway.
medicationSafety: Intraperitoneal antibiotic administration and exchange changes require dialysis-specific orders and competency.
teaching: Home PD patients should know that cloudy drainage or new abdominal pain requires prompt contact.
delegationScope: PD exchange responsibilities depend on training and setting; infection assessment/escalation requires licensed oversight.
examTrap: Assuming cloudy effluent is from diet or constipation and waiting until the next clinic visit.
oneLinePearl: Cloudy PD effluent is peritonitis until evaluated.

title: Peritoneal Dialysis Poor Outflow: Check Mechanics Before Forcing the System
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Poor peritoneal dialysis drainage can result from tubing kinks, position, constipation, catheter migration, or obstruction. Do not force fluid through a resistant system without following the dialysis troubleshooting protocol.
recognize: Slow/no drainage, incomplete output, abdominal fullness, or machine alarms are common cues.
priorities: Check tubing, clamps, positioning, and prescribed troubleshooting steps and escalate persistent outflow failure.
assessMonitor: Monitor inflow/outflow volume, abdominal symptoms, weight, edema, and constipation.
interventions: Reposition and correct external mechanical problems within training; do not manipulate the catheter invasively.
medicationSafety: Bowel-regimen medications may support PD function when prescribed; avoid unsupervised medication changes.
teaching: Patients should follow the home program's troubleshooting steps and know when to stop and call.
delegationScope: PD troubleshooting beyond basic mechanical checks requires dialysis-trained personnel.
examTrap: Applying pressure or forcing fluid through the catheter when drainage stops.
oneLinePearl: Check kinks and position—never force a resistant PD system.

title: Post-Dialysis Bleeding: Persistent Access Bleeding Needs Escalation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Bleeding from an AV access after needle removal should diminish with appropriate direct pressure. Persistent or recurrent bleeding requires assessment for anticoagulation effects, access problems, or coagulopathy.
recognize: Oozing beyond the expected period, expanding swelling, dizziness, hypotension, or recurrent bleeding after leaving dialysis are concerning.
priorities: Apply appropriate direct pressure without occluding access flow and escalate ongoing bleeding.
assessMonitor: Monitor bleeding amount, hemodynamics, access patency, medications, and symptoms of blood loss.
interventions: Use the dialysis unit's post-needle protocol and emergency services for uncontrolled hemorrhage.
medicationSafety: Review heparin exposure and chronic anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy when bleeding is prolonged.
teaching: Patients should know how to apply pressure and when bleeding requires emergency help.
delegationScope: Access-site pressure may be performed by trained personnel; evaluation of prolonged bleeding requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Using a tight circumferential wrap that stops access flow.
oneLinePearl: Stop the bleeding without stopping the access.

title: Missed Dialysis: Assess the Patient, Not the Calendar
bottomLine: A missed dialysis treatment is not automatically an emergency, but symptoms and laboratory risk can make it one. Assess dyspnea, edema, weakness, chest symptoms, mental status, and treatment history before deciding the next step.
recognize: Missed treatment increases risk for fluid overload, hyperkalemia, acidosis, and uremic symptoms.
priorities: Screen for respiratory distress, rhythm symptoms, severe weakness, confusion, or other deterioration and contact the dialysis team promptly.
assessMonitor: Review last dialysis, current symptoms, weight change, BP, oxygenation, and available labs.
interventions: Follow the dialysis center's urgent rescheduling/emergency referral pathway.
medicationSafety: Do not advise extra potassium binders, diuretics, or medication holds outside the prescribed action plan.
teaching: Patients should know whom to call immediately after a missed treatment and which symptoms require emergency care.
delegationScope: Scheduling can be administrative; clinical triage of symptoms requires licensed assessment.
examTrap: Telling a symptomatic patient simply to wait for the next available dialysis slot.
oneLinePearl: Missed dialysis becomes urgent when the patient becomes unstable.

title: Dialysis and Medication Timing: Treatment Can Change Drug Exposure
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hemodialysis can remove some medications and may change when certain drugs should be given. The PN/LVN should verify dialysis-day medication instructions rather than assuming routine timing is unchanged.
recognize: Drug dialyzability depends on properties such as protein binding, molecular size, distribution, and dialysis method.
priorities: Use the patient-specific dialysis medication schedule and clarify uncertain timing with pharmacy/dialysis team.
assessMonitor: Review dialysis timing, medication list, BP, glucose, and drug-specific monitoring needs.
interventions: Administer per the verified schedule and document omitted/delayed doses appropriately.
medicationSafety: Do not independently move all medications before or after dialysis based on a blanket rule.
teaching: Patients should keep an updated dialysis-day medication plan and not guess about skipped doses.
delegationScope: Medication timing verification is a licensed medication-safety responsibility.
examTrap: Assuming every medication should automatically be held before dialysis.
oneLinePearl: Dialysis-day medication timing is drug specific, not universal.
sourceBasis: FDA labeling and dialysis medication-management principles
